lead: No one has ever seen God, says John, but when we love one another God lives in us, and he has given us of his Spirit. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven at the hour of his glory and says what eternal life is: to know the Father and the One he has sent. In this week between the Ascension and Pentecost the two readings belong together. The Son has returned to the glory he had before the world began, and the Spirit he sends teaches us to know God by loving.

r.h: God is love; he has given us of his Spirit
set: The First Letter of John comes from the same circle as the Fourth Gospel. Tradition links it with the apostle John; many scholars think it was written by an elder of the community that treasured his teaching. It is written to churches shaken by a division: some had left (2:19), denying that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (4:2).
Against them the letter holds together three things: right faith in Jesus, love for one another, and the gift of the Spirit. Today’s passage weaves all three.
str: v. 12: no one has seen God; if we love, God lives in us.
vv. 13–16: how we know we abide in him: the Spirit, the confession of Jesus, love. “God is love.”
vv. 17–18: love made perfect gives boldness; perfect love casts out fear.
vv. 19–21: we love because he first loved us; no love for God without love for the brother or sister.
kw: The great word of John’s writings, used again and again in this passage. To abide is to stay, to make one’s home. God makes his home in us, and we in him.
“God is love” (vv. 8, 16). John does not say only that God loves, but that love is what God is. Love here is not first our feeling but God’s self-giving, seen in the sending of the Son (4:9–10).

The fear John speaks of “has to do with punishment”, the fear of a slave before a master. It is not the holy fear of God that Scripture praises as the beginning of wisdom. The more we love, the less we cower.
vv: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God lives in us, and his love is perfected in us.
The same words open the Gospel’s statement that the only Son has made the Father known (John 1:18). The God no one has seen becomes visible, in a way, in a community that loves.
God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them.
Perhaps the most famous sentence in the letter. It does not make love into God; it says that the God revealed in Jesus is love, and that whoever truly loves is living in him.
We love because he first loved us.

Textual note: some later manuscripts add an object, “we love him” or “we love God”. The shorter reading, followed by the NRSV, is wider: every true love in us, for God and for our neighbour, is an answer to his love.
ch: Pope Benedict XVI began his first encyclical with v. 16: “God is love, and those who abide in love abide in God, and God abides in them”; these words, he wrote, express with remarkable clarity the heart of the Christian faith (Deus Caritas Est 1). The Catechism teaches that God’s very being is love (CCC 221). St Augustine, preaching on this letter, gave his short rule, “Love, and do what you will”: when the root within is love, nothing but good can come from it (in substance, Homilies on the First Letter of John 7).

r.h: This is eternal life: that they may know you
set: The long discourse at the Last Supper (chapters 13–16) ends, and Jesus turns from his disciples to his Father. He prays aloud, first for himself (17:1–5), then for his disciples (17:6–19), then for all who will believe through their word (17:20–26). Christian tradition calls this the “priestly” prayer of Jesus (CCC 2747).

Throughout John’s Gospel the “hour” has been awaited. At Cana Jesus said, “My hour has not yet come” (2:4). Now he says, “the hour has come”. It is the hour of the Cross, which John sees as the hour of glory.
str: v. 1: Jesus looks up: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.”
v. 2: authority over all people, to give eternal life.
v. 4: the work on earth finished.
v. 5: the glory he had before the world existed.
kw: Not a clock hour, but the appointed time of the Father’s plan: the Passion, death, Resurrection and return to the Father, seen as one movement.
In the Old Testament God’s glory (kābôd) is his weighty, shining presence. In John the Cross is the place where that glory is most fully seen, because there love goes to the end (13:1).
Biblical knowing is not only information but personal communion. Eternal life is not a reward added after we know God; knowing him is eternal life, already begun.
vv: he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
The Son does not seek his own glory; he asks to be glorified so that he may glorify the Father. Their glory is one.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Some in the fourth century used this verse to deny that the Son is truly God. St Augustine answered that we should read it as one confession: that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, as the only true God (in substance, Tractates on John 105). The Son is named with the Father as the one whom to know is life.
So now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed.
The Son existed before the world, as the Prologue says (1:1). He asks to return to that glory, now as the Word made flesh. In the Ascension our human nature enters the glory of God with him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that when “his hour” came, Jesus prayed to the Father, and that this prayer of the hour fills the end times and carries them toward their consummation (CCC 2746–2749). Last Thursday we kept the Ascension; on Sunday the Spirit will come. Between them the Church prays with the Son’s own prayer: that we may know the Father, and so live.

study: John says that the God no one has seen becomes visible in our love for one another. Where can others see God in my family this week?
Jesus says eternal life is to know the Father. Am I growing in knowing God, or only in knowing about him?
